entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Canon Inc., founded 1937 in Tokyo by Takeshi Mitarai and Saburo Uchida as Precision Optical Instruments Laboratory, became Japan's leading camera manufacturer and then one of the world's dominant imaging technology companies — known for pioneering autofocus SLR cameras (Canon AE-1, 1976, the best-selling SLR in history), laser printing (Canon's laser engine powered the original HP LaserJet, 1984), and digital mirrorless camera systems (EOS R series). Canon's partnership with HP to create the laser printer industry is one of technology's most consequential corporate collaborations.

Canon's AE-1 (1976) was the first camera to use a microprocessor for automation control — the first mass-market affordable SLR with electronic automatic exposure. It sold 1 million units in the first two years, then 5 million total (twice the sales of any previous SLR) — the camera that democratized 35mm photography for amateur users. Canon's 1969 Canon F-1 professional system was the choice of photojournalists at the 1972 Munich Olympics.

The HP-Canon laser printing partnership (1984): Canon developed the compact laser engine; HP provided the computer interface and printer design. The HP LaserJet (1984) launched desktop laser printing for offices worldwide. Canon's laser engine continued powering HP LaserJets through dozens of generations, creating a licensing revenue stream that funded Canon's camera R&D. Canon's global workforce: 180,000 employees, ¥4 trillion annual revenue, operations in 200+ countries. The EOS R mirrorless system (2018) competes with Sony and Nikon for professional digital photography.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Canon — democratizing photography with the AE-1 and creating office laser printing through the HP partnership — participated in two of the most consequential democratizations of visual and document technology in the 20th century.
